utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before asking you to read the solemn oath, I need to know your identity. Will you tell me your first and last name, the date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vahid Karavelic. I was born in the village of Brezovik, Visoko municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 7th of April, 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession or occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are not active in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been working on this expert report for the past few months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But before, you must have been active. What was your last professional occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before starting work on the expert report, the previous four or five months I was living quietly as a retiree. I had retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you retired from what position and what profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After serving professionally in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what rank were you when you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the rank of major general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we address you as "general" today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General, will you please also tell the Chamber, in 1992/1993, which is more than 13 years ago, what were you doing? And if you were in the military, where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, at the beginning, when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina started, I was among the first to be appointed commander of the District Staff of Territorial Defence for the area of North-Eastern Bosnia, the district of Tuzla, until I was captured at the end of April of the same year, and then after being exchanged at the end of May of the same year I joined the staff as an operative, that is, the Republican Staff of Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then with the formation of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I remained in the same staff, until the 1st of September, 1992, as one of the operatives there. From the 1st of September, 1992 until August 1993, I performed the duty of deputy commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. And after that, from August 1993, I was the commander of that same corps, until August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. General, have you testified before in an international or national court of law about the facts of the events in your country in 1992/1993, or is this the first time for you to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Stanislav Galic case, were you a witness for the Prosecution or for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the national courts that you testified, were you a witness for the Prosecution, for the Defence, or an expert witness? What was your status? And do you remember the names of the cases in which you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were some sort of testimony in the form of statements given and not directly in the presence of the Prosecution or the Defence in a particular case. Among other things, I testified about certain events in the area of responsibility of my corps, such as the events in 1993, the case that we referred to as Caco and Celo, problems I had with brigades in my own corps, and in that connection I made statements and also in connection with a prison or detention centre that existed, again in my area of responsibility in Turcin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence, who will begin with their examination-in-chief, I wish to give you some information regarding the way in which the proceedings here have been planned for several days. As you know, you have been called by the Defence as an expert, and it is only in that capacity that you will be testifying. You're a military expert who will be answering questions put to you by the Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic and General Kubura, who felt that you should come and make your contribution to the establishment of the truth and to enlighten the Judges regarding certain points with respect to military command and other points that the Defence wishes to address. To do so, the Defence told you that they intend to question you for a period of about eight hours, which means that your testimony will spread over several days. We will begin today. I can tell you already that tomorrow you will not be coming because tomorrow we have another witness, who unfortunately has to be fitted in tomorrow. So perhaps today you could spend some time seeing the sights and benefitting from the fine weather tomorrow, and then you will be coming back on Wednesday and Thursday. Friday, as you know, is a UN holiday, as is Monday, so you will not be able to testify Friday or Monday, and we will resume the hearings on Tuesday. As I have said, the Defence will be asking you questions for a period of eight hours. Upon the completion of that phase, the Prosecution, which is seated to your right, will also have questions as part of the cross-examinations, and the -- and they tell us that may not take eight hours but a certain number of hours for their questions. Upon the completion of that stage too, the Defence counsel will have some additional questions for you directly linked to the questions put by the Prosecution. During these proceedings, documents may be shown to you and the Defence, which plans everything, has placed at your disposal binders of documents which will be shown to you either for you to comment on them as an expert or to make any other comments. The three Judges in front of you may, if they so wish, also ask you questions. As you are a military expert and as this is a case involving military men, it is quite possible that Judges will have questions for you too, either to clarify the documents or certain points covered during your testimony or because they feel in view of your status as an expert you may make some useful contributions in the interest of justice. And when the Judges put questions to you, without being partial to the thesis of the Defence or the Prosecution, the Judges will then allow the parties again to ask you questions and then both the Prosecution and the Defence will take the floor again to ask you questions for you to specify any points that you may have made answering the Judges' questions. Even though you are an expert, I need to draw your attention to two important points of our procedure: The first is that you have sworn to tell the whole truth, which excludes all false testimony, which is quite obvious; and the second point is of a purely technical nature, and that is that a witness may refuse to answer a question if he feels that one day his answer may be used against him to incriminate him. In this case, which is one we have never encountered so far, let me assure you, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer nevertheless but in this extremely exceptional case, the Chamber guarantees to the witness immunity from prosecution, so that these words cannot be used against him. This is a provision in our Rules which I wish to inform you about. Even though we have thousands of documents, this is basically an oral proceeding, so what counts are the words that you will speak. They are translated. You see a screen in front of you, which carries the English translation of your words, and it is these words that will represent the totality of your testimony, hence the importance of the answers you give to questions put to you. Should you not understand the meaning of a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it in clear terms, because it is important that your answers should be useful for the Judges because you are, of course, here for the Judges to be able to fully appreciate certain elements, which we are familiarised with through your report, but also through the answers you will give to the questions. So this adds importance to your oral testimony. As I have said, if you don't understand the meaning of a question, ask that it be rephrased for you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. During this hearing, for technical reasons we have to make breaks every hour and a half to give the interpreters a chance to rest, but also the technicians to be able to change the tapes, and also for you to have a rest, because as you will see, answering questions which can be highly technical can be quite tiring, and -- which means that you need to take a rest. Should you feel that you need longer breaks, let us know, because to answer questions hour after hour, as I have said, will be absolutely exhausting. I also count on Defence counsel not to shower you excessively with speedy questions, so that you can answer them normally. I also need to tell you - but the Defence will tell you too - as you will be speaking in your own language, make a pause before answering the questions so that the interpreters can interpret properly what you are saying into English and French. Those would be in very general terms how we intend to proceed over a period of some two weeks. I shall now give the floor to the Defence counsel, who will begin the examination-in-chief. And as the pulpit is in front of Mr. Bourgon, I assume that he will be the one conducting the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- myself and my colleague. My name is Stephane Bourgon. My colleague is Mrs. Residovic. And together we represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic. As you know, General, this testimony of yours applies to both accused, and I take this opportunity to introduce also my colleagues in the back, Mr. Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and also Mr. Nermin Mulalic, who represent General Kubura. Together we represent the accused, and I have some questions to ask you concerning your expert report, which has now been admitted before the Trial Chamber as Exhibit 2088. As you have heard me mention to the Presiding Judge, I believe that we will be spending together the next 10 hours or so. And as you can imagine, I have a number of topics I would like to address with you. Before I begin, however, I would like to ask you a few questions on your military experience and your military background. Even though you did enclose your biography with your expert report, I think it is important that we cover some of the positions that you have occupied in order to establish your background as an expert. I would first like to begin by the period of your military career from the beginning until the time you deserted from the JNA, and I believe you deserted from the JNA in 1991. Can you, General, briefly describe the positions you held from the beginning of your career until 1991.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I completed my secondary education in Visoko in 1975. From that year on, I am a soldier and a member of the Yugoslav People's Army. In 1979, I graduated from the military academy in Belgrade. From 1979 until 1982, I served as a commander of a platoon in the infantry educational centre of the JNA in Bileca. From 1982, after being transferred, I was commander of an infantry company in Slovenia, in Pivka, close to the Italian border. From 1985 until 1988, I completed a six-month course in Sarajevo for the position of battalion commander in the JNA. At the same time, that is, in 1988, I was appointed commander of the motorised brigade in -- battalion in Slovenia, and I performed that duty until 1991. At the end of 1991, in mid-December, I deserted from the Yugoslav People's Army, from the barracks in Tuzla, having the rank of captain first class, even though while serving as battalion commander in 1989 I passed the final examination for the rank of major in Belgrade. And I omitted to mention something that may be important, and that is that in 1991, after the attack by the Yugoslav People's Army against the Republic of Slovenia on the 26th of June, shortly after that, that is, on the 20th of August that same year, together with my unit, I was relocated from Ljubljana to the central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the barracks in Zenica. Two months after that, I was relocated with my unit from the Zenica barracks to a new barracks in North-Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Tuzla. And in mid-December, it was from there that I deserted.

utterances.text: Welcome back, General. Just before this technical break, you informed the Trial Chamber of your military activities during the period from the time you joined in 1975 until the time you deserted the JNA in 1991. I would now like you to -- to ask you to tell us why you deserted the JNA at that time.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I said that I was a member of the JNA from 1975 until the end of 1991. Right up until 1991, I felt that the JNA really was my army. In 1991, numerous problems arose probably as a result of what had happened in the 1990s, over the last few years, the results of political problems in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In 1991, when Slovenia was attacked, on the 26th of June, I said that I was the commander of a motorised battalion at the time and I saw and observed many things, and I must admit that I was very surprised by what I saw. From day to day, from the summer of 1991 onwards, the JNA was heading in one direction. Its interest was to fight for one of the peoples in the former Yugoslavia, that is to say, for the Serbian people. This is something that I felt, among other things, in many of the activities carried out in the battalion. I had a lot of officers, members of various ethnic communities from the former Yugoslavia, and the relation to the Serbian officers was different with regard to the relation to officers of other ethnic communities. When I moved from Ljubljana to Zenica on 20th of August of that year, I had a deputy, an officer, who was three or four years younger than me. His name was Vinko Pandurevic. And under no circumstances could he go to the command staff academy in Belgrade before me. But when we arrived in Zenica, without any explanations he left his as my deputy and went to the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade. Then the non-Serbian officers started leaving and soon the soldiers started leaving. When I was transferred two months later, on the 20th of October, to Tuzla in order to be sent with the battalion to engage in combat in Vukovar, in the north-eastern part of Croatia, where I was to replace a battalion that had already been sent there from the barracks in Tuzla, in the course of those preparations -- and I'll provide you with one example: I was woken up by the noise in the Tuzla barracks. When I woke up, I went outside, joined the mass of troops outside, and I could see with my very own eyes that there were many soldiers with signs on their caps that we called cockades. Among them, I could see my deputy, Vinko Pandurevic. And, in fact, when leaving for Belgrade, the Command Staff academy ceased to function then. He was deployed. He took a unit from the central part of Serbia, and took them to Knin in the Republic of Croatia to engage in combat there. And that evening he was just passing through Tuzla, and it was at that time, although I had previously had occasion to have such experience, it was at that time that I finally realised that the JNA was no longer my army, that the JNA was not defending my interests as one of the citizens of the former Yugoslavia. Shortly after that event, I deserted and left the JNA. Up until that point in time, up until the time when I deserted, over 70, even 80 per cent of all the officers and soldiers of non-Serbian ethnicity had already deserted my battalion. It's difficult to provide you with a number, but it was between 70 and 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, after deserting the JNA in 1991, what exactly did you do? And if you did join a different army, what positions did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When I deserted the JNA in mid-December 1991, I wanted -- a list was printed for me. I started looking for a new job for a certain period of time. While looking for a new job, I was sent to look for another job through my father and other friends in the police. When looking for a job - and I thought I had found a job - when looking for a job, I attended a meeting towards the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992 with Sefer Halilovic and Karisik Kemo. These two people were at the head of the Patriotic League here that had to a certain extent already been established. I was asked whether I wanted to participate in the preparations or to participate in preparing the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina to mount the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina if Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked. I accepted that. And after a certain period of time in January 1992, they sent me to be a coordinator in North-Eastern Bosnia, in the Tuzla area. And in January, February, and March, that was where I worked as a coordinator of the Patriotic League for the Tuzla area that covered the territory of 19 municipalities. I tried to establish contact with individuals and prepare all the citizens of that area to mount a defence if an attack was carried out on Bosnia and Herzegovina. I continued doing this until the 6th of April, 1992, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by the International Community, and shortly afterwards, on the 12th of April, 1992, when a new Territorial Defence for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established and when its Republican Staff was established, I was appointed as commander of the Tuzla District Staff -- or rather, of the north-eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to you personally after you became the commander of the District Territorial Defence Staff in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Up until then, I was in that area. From time to time I received certain instructions from political -- from the political leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I visited municipalities in the territory of North-Eastern Bosnia and I established contact with all the citizens in order to ensure that they would establish contact with people, with citizens, so that if Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked, they might be prepared to a certain extent and ready to defend their villages, their houses, their towns, and finally their state. On the 1st of April, 1992, when Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked -- or rather, Bijeljina was attacked, which is a town in the north-eastern corner of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when Arkan's men entered that town, I tried to defend it. I wasn't successful in doing so. And after Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised on the 6th of April, two days after its recognition, on the 8th of April, 1992, an even fiercer attack was launched on Zvornik, which is more to the south of Bijeljina, and it is also at the border with the Republic of Serbia. I defended that town for a full three weeks. And on the 26th of April, it fell. We failed to defend it. In the meantime, on the 12th of April, I was appointed as the commander of the Regional Staff of the Tuzla Territorial Defence, and then on the following day, on the 27th of April, 1992, since in North-Eastern Bosnia there was still a lot of units in JNA barracks in Tuzla and around Tuzla and in other towns, the political and military situation was very confused and uncertain and couldn't be predicted. And given various circumstances, in response to Osmo Dzudzakovic's [phoen] appeal to come to a meeting with him at 12.00, because of problems at the military airport, Zivinice near Tuzla - their movement had been blocked and supplies had been blocked for their forward post - I went to that meeting. The deputy commander, Major Pracar, was in his office with two military policemen. When I entered there, I was captured, disarmed, and rapidly taken to the Dubrava airport, and then I was transferred by helicopter in Belgrade that very same afternoon, and then I was transferred from Belgrade in a vehicle to a prison in Sremska Mitrovica. I remained in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica until the 9th of May. I was processed there by three colonels. Finally, I was informed that I would probably be given the death penalty, that I was asked how I would like to be executed. I said that I would like to be executed by a firing squad. And suddenly on the 9th of May I was transferred to Belgrade again, and then I was transferred by helicopter from Belgrade to Pale in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to Pale, above Sarajevo. On the 13th of May, 1992, I was exchanged at Stup, a place in the town of Sarajevo. I was exchanged thanks to an event that occurred on the 2nd of May, 1992 in Sarajevo. Then Alija Izetbegovic was captured by the JNA. He was at the airport. He was captured. He was arrested when returning from negotiations in Geneva. When he was exchanged with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander of the second military area, General Kukanjac, there was the famous event of the 2nd of May in Sarajevo on which occasion about 200 JNA officers were captured, one of whom was a key officer, one of the assistants of General Aco Vasiljevic, who was the top man in the security service in the JNA. To get their officers back, I had the opportunity of being exchanged, although I knew nothing about this affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like now to ask you what happened after you were exchanged. But there is one issue you did mention, called the Patriotic League. And I would simply like to ask you to provide, if you can, further information on the Patriotic League. When did you join this organisation? What is it and what happened to the Patriotic League once Bosnia and Herzegovina became a sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The Patriotic League was an informal political and military organisation. It hadn't been organised or structured in any particular way. It was an organisation that people would join exclusively on a voluntary basis. Through the work of the Patriotic League and through certain meetings held at high levels, certain conclusions were adopted. In all those conclusions, in all the assessments that were made, it was stated that the Patriotic League was being organised in case Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked. At one of those meetings or at one of those briefings, held on the 6th and 7th of February in the village of Mehurici, commanders of Regional Staffs of the Patriotic League were assembled. This meeting went on for 24 hours in one of the houses and the conclusion and the platform, if that's what we can call it, which is a document contained among the documents we have here, says that the Patriotic League must be organised to a certain level for one basic reason, because Bosnia and Herzegovina will most probably be attacked. Its organisation should include all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and its main objective in the case of an attack, and if it is necessary to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, its main objective is to -- is for it to be transferred into the future defence force for Bosnia and Herzegovina. It should defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, a country that belongs to all its citizens, regardless of all the differences among its people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And when you became the commander of the District Territorial Defence Staff in Tuzla or after the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what happened to the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state on the 6th of April, 1992, as early as the 8th of April, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued a decree according to which the name of the republic was to be changed. At the same time, the old Republican Staff of the Socialist Republic was to be disbanded and a new Republican Territorial Defence Staff for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be established. On the following day, a new decree was issued, according to which an armed force was being established under the name of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that decree, the following was stated, among other things: Any armed forces in existence to that -- up until that point in time had to join the Republican Regional or -- and Municipal Staffs -- or rather, they had to join the command of those staffs at those three levels, and they had to be placed under the unified command of the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The deadline to do this was the 15th of April, 1992. Whoever failed to place themselves within that chain of command would be subject to legal sanctions. After the 15th of April, 1992, the Patriotic League no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, can you briefly describe the state you were in when you were exchanged in Sarajevo and what exactly you did after being exchanged.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When I was exchanged on the 13th of May, 1992 in Sarajevo, I first spent some time in the hospital in order to recover from the consequences of the time I had spent in prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Then I joined the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence under the command of General Hasan Efendic, the first commander of the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence. After Sefer Halilovic had assumed his duties -- after Hasan Efendic had assumed his duties, I continued to perform these duties and I continued to work in the staff in that position, and then when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, I remained one of the operative officers in the staff up until the 1st of September, 1992, which is when I was appointed as the deputy commander of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I read from your biography, which is attached to your report, that in September, as you say, of 1992 you became the deputy commander of the 1st Corps, that you then became the commander of the corps in July 1993, and that you remained in this position until August of 1995, when you became the commander of the West Bosnia Command, and that at that moment or towards the end of 1995 you were appointed as the chief operative administrator for politics, planning, and operations of the joint command of the Bosnia federation army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But during 1995, among other things, for a short period of time I served as commander of the West Bosnia Command in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And according to your biography, in 1993 you were promoted brigadier general, and in 1999 promoted major general in the federation army. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In December 1993, to the rank of brigadier general; and in July 1999, to the rank of major general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your career, General, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you attended any training or any courses on either military command or management.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the post-war period, I was sent to attend a large number of courses and seminars organised by NATO and other international organisations. Among other things, from December 1997 until May 1999, for a year and a half almost, I stayed in the United States of America, for a while in San Antonio, Texas, and the rest of the time in Monterrey in the Marines' postgraduate school, and attended courses there entitled "Material management," that is, the use of the country's resources for the country's defence. Then I participated in many NATO courses; among others, a course in Garmisch Parten Kirchen, and then a number of other such courses in Norway, Croatia, Germany, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your biography --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: And a large number of seminars organised by the Partnership for Peace that were held from time to time, and they overlapped or followed on to the previous courses that I mentioned. All these courses and this postwar training up until the time I retired were devoted to senior management and the establishment of peace in the period of the former Yugoslavia, or broader than that, in the Balkans and Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In your biography, it is stated that you obtained a masters degree, a Masters of Science, in 1992 at the University of Sarajevo at the Faculty of Political Science. Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No, not in 1992 but in 2002. That must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is what it is -- this is your biography in the expert report. That says "1992." So did you obtain a masters degree? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I did obtain a masters degree at the Faculty of Political Science in Sarajevo in 2002, in the month of July. And I obtained the title of Master of Political Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, did you write a thesis as part of your masters degree? And if so, what was the title or the subject of your thesis?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The title of my masters thesis was "Political and military preparations for the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina and their implementation in the area of North-Eastern Bosnia, 1991-1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your diary appears -- sorry, your biography also states that you were awarded the Golden Model of Bosnia and Herzegovina for your contribution to the Patriotic League and also the Order of the Golden Coat of Arms with Swords for your service in the army. Can you confirm having received those two awards?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: If I may add, I received many tokens of tribute during my life and work in the Yugoslav People's Army as well, while in the Patriotic League it is true that I received the Golden Relief of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, this cannot be said to have been awarded by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina but by a lower-level body, and the Order with the Coat of Arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina with Golden Swords was the order that I received in 1997, awarded by the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina for my contribution to the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period from 1992 to 1995. And in the postwar period, I was awarded on several other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, in your expert opinion, you quoted a book which I believe you have written. Can you briefly tell us what this book is and when it was written.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I published a book entitled "The aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1991-1992." That book is actually the result and product of my masters thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, before I move on to my first topic, General, given that you were the commander of the 1st Corps, I would like you to briefly describe the situation you were in as the commander of the 1st Corps in 1993 and following.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: 1992 and 1993 in Sarajevo, where at first I was a member of the Republican Staff of the TO and then deputy commander of the 1st Corps and then, in 1993, the commander of the 1st Corps, and what is important for the second half of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 is that the situation in Sarajevo could be described as follows: That the political system of the state to a high percentage - it is difficult to say exactly to what extent, was it 60, 70, or 80 per cent - had been destroyed and did not exist as such. The country's defence system could be described similarly or even worse than that, for one simple reason, that most of the Serb population had left the political structures of the state, as well as the military defence structures, and all of this was accompanied by an exodus of the Croat population as well, though in smaller numbers. This shows that from the standpoint of the organisation of the defence of the city of Sarajevo during the summer of 1992, the situation was extremely confused, disoriented, that one hardly knew who was giving orders and who was supposed to carry out those orders, who was where. There was no interconnection between numerous and, let me say, diverse units that were formed immediately in April 1992 in streets, in districts, on various -- in various parts of the city of Sarajevo; whereas, the enemy, even before April 1992, had taken control of positions around the town of Sarajevo of all dominant features, so that the town of Sarajevo, as the capital of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was completely encircled and blocked, so that only birds could leave or enter the town of Sarajevo. Simultaneously with the encirclement and blockade of the town of Sarajevo there were still many barracks full of soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army. Among them there were good interconnections, and in view of the spread of hostile groups in the town of Sarajevo, as the overall objective was in a brief period of time, in a matter of days or weeks, to act simultaneously from the outside and from the inside, the barracks and its forces deployed within the city of Sarajevo, and by combined action for the town to be brought into an impasse, for it to capitulate, or, rather, for the political leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time to be toppled and for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be proclaimed a component part of a new Yugoslavia or, in other words, of a greater Serbia. The key point of this period was the 2nd of May, that I referred to a moment ago. Later, during the summer of 1992, the District Staff of the Territorial Defence of the city of Sarajevo, which was functioning at the time, headed by Mustafa Hajrulahovic, nicknamed Talijan, endeavoured to link together numerous and diverse small units and all this was very difficult to achieve because all those units needed to be linked up. The units had to be enlarged, and a single chain of command established. And when we formed the 1st Corps on the 1st of September, 1992 and when a number of people were immediately appointed to the 1st Corps command, we had to work hard and long to achieve that. However, progress was evident as time passed, but I can say with full responsibility that this process was not completed satisfactorily until perhaps the end of the next year, that is, 1993, which only shows how complicated and complex an issue this was, that is, the issue of organising and defending the town of Sarajevo as the centre of the country and of the state, because had the city of Sarajevo fallen, that would have most probably marked the end of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, given what you have just mentioned, with respect to the consequences, had the city of Sarajevo capitulated to the enemy, I would like to ask you: From a corps commander's perspective, what were your priorities and what were your goals and how was it to be a corps commander in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: If I may put it simply: If the war were ever to be repeated, I would never at any cost agree to take on such a position. In those days, for me as deputy commander of the 1st Corps and later as the commander, my main priority was to establish contacts as soon as possible with all those numerous units in the city of Sarajevo that I just mentioned or -- also, outside the city of Sarajevo, as the 1st Corps also had responsibility beyond the actual circumference of the city of Sarajevo itself. And then once contact is established with those units, to unite them to form larger units, because that is the only way to conduct a struggle successfully, that is, to achieve defence. I must admit that there were numerous situations that I personally and my command managed to deal with that I myself was not aware of probably due to luck. I can give you just a few examples. When forming these larger units out of smaller ones, what was our main problem? The problem lay in the fact that these numerous units had been formed on a voluntary basis, so that in each street or maybe district of Sarajevo an individual would achieve some sort of authority and he would rally units around him, and that is how a unit was formed. Whether it was called a platoon, a squad, or a company, or a detachment, later battalions, and so on. The question never arose nor was it possible to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ask whether those people were qualified and capable to lead such units; however, when the time came to unite units, to form larger ones, it was very difficult to talk to these people, and in many situations almost impossible to tell this person that his unit, be it a platoon or a detachment or a company, have to join into a higher-level unit, and that someone else would be his superior, because many such people considered themselves to be untouchable. The only people who had the ability to lead, they had men following them and they thought they could do whatever they wanted. For a long time, this situation had it repercussions throughout the city of Sarajevo in 1992 and to a great extent in 1993 as well. By hard work and tireless efforts, this transformation was carried out. There was simultaneous transformation of units with simultaneous daily contact in order to defend the city of Sarajevo. During 1992, the focus of the aggressor's forces around Sarajevo was to cut the city of Sarajevo into several parts because they realised that it would be hard, or they soon realised that it would be hard for them to capture the city, as it was an urban inhabited area, and according to all principles of military science, the most difficult kind of combat is in inhabited areas. And that is why they wanted to cut up the town into parts and then stifle one by one. Shortly after that, we encountered very serious problems with food, water, armaments, ammunition, communications means, and everything else that is necessary for a formation such as a corps; in this case, the 1st Corps. By tireless daily struggle and through incessant efforts by all, the struggle was waged and the forces were organised and enlarged, and these activities continued into 1993, and I can say on this occasion that I just managed to achieve a satisfactory level of organisation of my corps in October or maybe November 1993, because in October, by force of arms, I placed under my command two of my brigades, which had tried to break off from the command, and shortly after that, at the beginning of November 1993, a Croatian brigade, called King Tvrtko, or rather, an HVO brigade, which was in Sarajevo but not under my command, I managed to place by force of command that brigade too under my command and within my chain of command so as to have a united struggle for the defence of the capital of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I just have one very quick question before moving on, and that is: How many subordinates did you have as commander of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was one of the largest corps in 1993. Let me speak about halfway into the war. I had three operative groups, each group consisting of five, six, seven brigades, and a number of independent units. For the sake of an example, in the summer of 1993 the 1st Corps numbered more than 75.000 men. If I were to tell you how many officers it had, lower level, senior level, non-commissioned officers, that would be hard for me to give you the figures now. I had a lot of people linked to me along the chain of command, and it was very difficult for me to command the 1st Corps of the ABiH during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, based on your experience as the commander of the 1st Corps defending the city of Sarajevo during the war, bearing in mind your experience in the JNA from 1975 to 1991, and considering the years you spent after the war in the Army of the Federation as the then-chief of operations and training, do you feel, General, that you are qualified to testify on as an expert witness on the exercise of command in the military at senior levels?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That's a difficult question for me because I wouldn't like to speak about myself, so it's hard for me to give you a direct and short answer. However, I accepted to prepare this expert report precisely because of what I have said up to now, in fact, believing that what I have experienced in the course of my career and especially bearing in mind the fact that I exercised the duty of commander of the 1st Corps, which in my view was a very complicated and difficult assignment, I believe that I would be able to present arguments, facts, and descriptions of all the events covered by the report and also through answering questions put to me in this room, that my answers and my comments about the actual events and how they took place and when and what the overall situation was like, that these answers may be of considerable usefulness to the Trial Chamber in their further determinations and assessments of everything covered by the expert report and answers to questions put to me here. This is what guided me and prompted me to accept this assignment, and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, as you know, one of the accused in this case is General Hadzihasanovic, and you know that General Hadzihasanovic was the commander of the 3rd Corps during part of the period during which you were the commander of the 1st Corps in the same army. My question to you is: Do you believe that it is possible for you to be independent enough to offer an objective military expert opinion in this case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: With reference to what I have just said, I believe that I could say yes in response to your question. In most of my responses to the questions put to me and in accordance with what I put down in the annexes, there are arguments presented on the actions that I had to take as a corps commander, among other things, and I was in a very similar situation, if not in an identical situation, to that of the commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps. And I would repeat my conclusion that in the explanations I provide of all of these events and in the explanations of all the duties and obligations that I had as a corps commander and that all others had in the chain of command, but also with reference to the duties and obligations of superiors and of the state, whose duty it was to provide an operative unit such as a corps with many things, with reference to all of these facts I will try to depict the truth of the events -- I'll try to depict what actually happened, and I hope that this will be of much assistance to this Trial Chamber. And in my opinion, I don't think that there's a direct relation. I don't think whether I can be sufficiently objective or neutral with regard to the 3rd Corps commander is an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, how well do you know General Hadzihasanovic and for how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I have known -- or rather, I met General Hadzihasanovic for the first time in July -- or in June or July of 1992 in the staff of the General Staff of the ABiH in Sarajevo because in the summer of 1992 we were there as operative officers for a certain period of time. We were both there at the same time. From that point in time onwards, we would occasionally be closer to each other; however, we weren't often in the immediate vicinity of each other. As operative officers in that staff up until -- we were there until the 1st of September, 1992, and then as of the 1st of September, 1992 we were appointed to the command of the 1st Corps of the ABiH. He remained there in the command of the 1st Corps for two to three months, I think -- for two months. And at the beginning of November 1993, he left the 1st Corps command and went to Central Bosnia, where he assumed other duties, so that in the course of the war in 1993 and in 1994 we did not see each other very often. When he was appointed to a higher-level duty later on, when he was appointed as Chief of Staff in the Main Staff of the ABiH, occasionally in the course of 1995 we had more frequent contact, but through the chain of command, which is a result of the structure and organisation of the ABiH. And in the post-war period, we would occasionally see each other, but rarely. I think that General Hadzihasanovic respects me and I respect him too. We aren't close friends. Our families did not visit each other. We would only see each other occasionally and, in fact, fairly rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have one last question for you, General, concerning your military background: I see from everything that you have told us today that you have been a battalion commander and that after being commander of the District Territorial Defence Staff, you went on to become a corps commander. So, in fact, I don't think that you ever held the position, for example, of brigade commander. Now, do you think that this is something missing in your experience in order to be able to assist the Trial Chamber in this case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the career of each and every officer, passing through all the command levels has a certain importance. It's important to have various command duties, until the officer becomes a general and has certain extremely important, not the say the most important, military duties to perform. However, I believe that establishment duties are extremely important. A commander of a company, the commander of a battalion has very important duties to perform. I couldn't say that the established -- establishment duty of a brigade commander is not very important. On the contrary. And since afterwards I was immediately appointed as the 1st Corps commander, the lack of experience as a brigade commander is something that I think that I compensated for being -- by performing the duties of an operative officer in the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence -- or rather, in the Main Staff of the ABiH in the course of the summer of 1992. And in addition, I performed the duties of deputy commander of the 1st Corps for one year. I believe that those duties that I performed compensated perhaps for my lack of experience. However, this is quite justified in wartime conditions, and I personally believe that in terms of military knowledge, military experience, in terms of what I went through in the course of the war, this did not post a significant problem. The fact that I never performed the duties of a brigade commander was never a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was put to you by the Presiding Judge. You answered that you had been working for some time on the preparation of this expert report. And I note that in the first part you explain how this report was written. Can you explain to us how and -- how you went about to draft this report.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In August of last year, towards the end of August of last year, I retired and I ceased to work -- or to be a member of the military. Even before I ceased working in the military, Mrs. Residovic requested that she see me to speak to me in her office in Sarajevo. We spoke about whether I would agree to start work on preparing to draft this report. I'm not sure, but I don't think I immediately accepted the offer. There was another meeting, at which I accepted the offer. At the same time, while I was still a member of the military, I started working on this expert report. After I had retired, I got more involved in working on this expert report. I must admit that all the work carried out to draft this report was very difficult and not gratifying because of the extensive nature of the questions and everything else that I was requested to analyse, review, read, et cetera, et cetera. I worked insistently over the last few months of last year. I made a first draft of the expert report, which consisted of over 200 pages, if I'm not mistaken. And then I was asked to shorten the report, to reduce it to 150 pages or less, which is what I did. On a number of occasions, I had forwards meetings with Mrs. Residovic and yourself or I had contact with Mrs. Residovic and yourself in the course of preparing this report, and this continued until the final version of the report was ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, did you receive any assistance in the period during which you drafted this report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Indeed I did. For the most part, I worked alone with three assistants of mine: A typist, an assistant to help me with the graphics, with computer graphics. Mrs. Residovic's office in Sarajevo provided me with much help, together with General Mustafa Polutak, and as far as all these documents are concerned that are in the binders to the right and with many other documents, I was provided with much assistance. I also received a lot of assistance from many other individuals, in terms of using documents from the archives of the Federation army, et cetera, et cetera. I was then provided with all the documents from the Prosecution, from the Defence, and I read through these documents, used them when drafting the final version of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I see beside you that you have a number of binders of an orange colour, and the Presiding Judge mentioned to you at the beginning that those were provided to you by the Defence. But can you explain what these documents are, who has prepared them, and what they are exactly.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The documents that are to my right are in fact all the documents registered by the Defence and the Prosecution at this Tribunal. I prepared most of the documents myself, but many documents were prepared by the office of Mrs. Residovic, headed by Mr. Polutak. In these annexes, we have all the documents which have been filed on the basis of their dates, on the basis of the events depicted. If some documents couldn't be filed within certain categories, they were placed in a binder the title of which was "miscellaneous" or "other documents." In each of these binders -- on each of the binders, on the spine of each binder, we have the -- we have reference to the group of documents, the dates of the documents, or the period that the documents concern, and on the first page of each of these binders we have a list of the documents that follows the way they were registered here before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, General, how many documents approximately are contained in these binders and whether you read all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: There are a lot of documents. When we calculated the number of documents, I think that according to the results obtained, there are over 5.000 pages. I haven't read all of them for a very simple reason: At one point in time, I came to the conclusion that it was quite simply impossible. But I have read the vast majority of these documents. The ones that I have not read are documents that I at least had a look at when preparing this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And I'd like now to address quickly the issue of the annexes to your report. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how these annexes were prepared and what was your aim in preparing all these annexes.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the annexes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, the annexes to the report.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Apart from the expert report, I also prepared 108 annexes. And if I add another three new annexes to that number, 111 annexes. They are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. all referred to in the expert report, and the objective of these annexes is to clarify a lot of definitions provided and the various breakdowns or diagrams provided are there to visually explain the actual contents of the expert report. All of these annexes are probably on the computer at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, looking through these annexes, I noticed that some annexes are provided with the report but not referred to in the report. And I also noticed that there were gaps in the numbering of the annexes. Can you explain how that can be?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can give you an example, if you want, of a -- for example -- well, I -- do you understand what I mean by the fact that there are annexes in the report but they're not referred to in the report?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Well, in the second version of the expert report, I think that I also provided the final breakdown of the annexes, of all the annexes that were part of one of the versions of the report. Subsequently corrections were made. When there was a translation from the Bosnian language into the English and then a translation from the English back into the Bosnian, and there were many corrections and, in fact, certain sections were completely deleted or certain sections were added. And when certain sections were deleted, it was also necessary to automatically delete certain annexes. And so as not to make a new register of all the annexes in the report itself - that would have been a very slow and complicated procedure - we have these gaps in the list of annexes. These gaps appear on a number of occasions. There's the number of an annex but there's no annex. And then some annexes remained at the end, which I excluded from the report, in the sense that it's been registered in the report, in the contents of the report. This was because I couldn't decide if the annexes needed -- if the annexes are needed, they're there, and they can be used too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the questions you answered or the questions that were provided to you to draft your expert opinion, you mentioned a little earlier something like the ungratifying nature of the questions or something like that. Can you tell us who provided you with these questions and how you went about to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning, from the very first meeting with Mrs. Residovic, when I accepted this challenge, I received the first version of the questions that I was to answer -- or rather, these were the questions that I was to use to prepare and draft my expert report. After a month or two, the questions themselves were amended. Certain questions were added; others were deleted. Mrs. Residovic and you yourself provided me with these amended questions. And finally, given the translation needs, in February the final corrections were made because there were certain discrepancies because of the translation into the English and then translating it back into the Bosnian language. There were certain discrepancies in the way that certain thoughts had been formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One last question with respect to the preparation of the report. I would just like to know: How much time, looking back, you spent on the preparation of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That's another difficult question. I think that this is really an all-encompassing report, a report that required a lot of time. It was difficult for one man to draft this report without having recourse to assistance. It was a report that involved reading a lot of documents. It was a report that involved consulting various sources. It involved consulting military rules and many books that could be used as sources for drafting this report. I believe that it took at least four months -- that would be the minimum period of time required to draft this report with the assistance of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... prepared this report. Is this something that you'd done -- that you completed as a paid assignment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Until now, I have not received a single penny. Now, whether something will come in the future, that depends on you. But may I also add: In regard to a commander in a wartime, when I said I wouldn't accept it, I don't know whether I would ever again agree to accept such an assignment as this one was to prepare this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... more precise: Is it an assignment for which you will be paid and that you accepted to perform in exchange for remuneration?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a quarter past 5.00. We will resume at about 20 to 6.00 or a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We'll wait a few minutes for the witness because I think the Prosecution wishes to take the floor. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution feels duty-bound to draw to the Trial Chamber's attention the fact that it appeared from where we're sitting that the witness during the course of his oral testimony is referring to some kind of handwritten notes. When he first took the stand, it -- it appeared that he had his written report in front of him, which is not in and of itself, of course, problematic for expert witnesses, but it then became clear during the course of his testimony that interspersed among his copy of the report is a number of pages with lined -- lined paper pages with handwriting and highlighters on it. I'm not in any way implying that anything improper has taken place. I simply felt duty-bound to inform the Trial Chamber that it does appear that the witness has some kind of handwritten note -- notes, the pages of which have been interspersed in his copy of the -- of the -- of his own expert report that he has before him. And I simply wanted to draw that to the Chamber's attention, of course, in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you surely prepared your witness and explained to him that the procedure is such that he has to have his report and his annexes but not additional documents drafted in advance. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I know, Mr. President, is that he noted things in his report, and I was wondering whether I should ask him the question, because I noticed too that he seemed to be looking at something. So I was going to ask him the question myself. I know he has his report and his documents. While we were working together during the weekend, he was taking notes. Now, if the Prosecution wishes those notes to be withdrawn and replaced by a clean report, I have no problems with that. It's up to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, perhaps we could ask the witness what are the notes he has, because if these are pages from his report, there shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That might very well be the easiest course of action. Again, Mr. President, I did not, however, that there are pages with lined paper with hand -- extensive handwriting, including portions that have been highlighted with a yellow highlighter. And I -- I simply felt that it was my duty to inform the Trial Chamber, and I did inform the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so we're going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just before I give the floor again to Defence counsel, he is going to ask you a question about the documents you have in front of you. So I'll give the floor to Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Welcome back, General. I would just like to ask you one question before we continue in respect of the documents that you have with you, because we saw that you've been looking at something while giving your answers, and we're wondering what exactly you have with you today in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In my briefcase, I only have my mobile phone, some pens and pencils, and a CD. And here I have the expert report that I prepared, and at the beginning of the report are 10 or 15 pages of my notes, various notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, when you say "notes that I took," what are these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Notes resulting from the conversations I had with Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these are notes that you made after the interviews you had with the attorneys; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part of them, yes and part of them I made myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But do you need those notes to answer questions, or could you put them aside and look only at the report and its attachments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be preferable that we remove the notes, so long as he can keep his report though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, if you could just separate the notes from your report and just keep with you your report. And I would like to know, General, if the report you have is the report that you had when you were working with me with all the annotations on it, the -- I saw you were making red lines in your report. Is that what you have with you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend is satisfied, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution? Yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, we are a bit late in -- in the time I had planned for the examination-in-chief, so maybe I will ask you to try and keep your answers a little shorter, where possible of course, but I don't want to refrain you from saying what you would like to say. And my first question deals with the report itself. Is there, having worked all this time on this expert report, is there one issue that stands out from all the work you have done which you could highlight for the Trial Chamber in analysing the exercise of command by both accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In accordance with my expert report and the questions analysed in that report, in accordance with what the questions put to me required, my general observations and confirmation of certain definitions from sources or documents of that period, I would highlight two facts which are lacking and which are very important for the exercise of the functions of a senior officer or leader: In order to complement the report or my reflections about the issue, I think sufficient space has not been devoted to the concept of reality, as to what things were like with respect to the overall political and military situation during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. When I say "reality," what I mean is that one should bear in mind -- when answering the vast majority of those questions, one should bear in mind that reality and that reality was extremely hard, a reality characterised by disorganisation or, rather, the absence of a political and defensive system at the beginning of the war, a situation that in a nutshell was extremely, extremely confusing in every sense and in every aspect of the social order and, more specifically, the system of defence. That is one point and one fact. Another which I would also like to highlight is that one needs to bear in mind the fact of the nature of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this fact reflecting the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the conflict, had an extremely adverse and negative effect on the mission of each and every commander or military leader, and especially the mission of a senior military leader. By way of example, let me point out that in my opinion - and I am firmly convinced of this - that it would be difficult, very difficult, to find another example from wars in the world in the past with a situation similar to the one in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period from 1992 to 1995 when government forces of the internationally recognised State of Bosnia and Herzegovina were virtually in every respect in a less favourable position than all the other forces, retrograde forces or secessionist forces, et cetera, et cetera, and that those government forces in 1993 were waging a battle against three enemies, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question deals with the assessment of the work performed by a senior commander in a war situation. What would be in your view the most important factor to bear in mind when looking at the work performed by a senior commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The most important and key factor to be borne in mind for every senior commander is his mission. Every senior leader is entrusted with a mission by his superior, or more specifically, from the political and military state leadership. Everything else comes second to the mission of that senior military leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And when we look at the ability of a senior military commander to make decisions and to exercise his command, can you mention some of the factors which will influence the decision-making of a senior commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the first place, I would say when making any decision, a senior military leader is influenced by everything, absolutely everything that is going on in the area in that territory, in whatever shape or form, has a more or less direct effect on the mission of a senior military commander. As to the factors that would most directly influence the mission, I would list them as follows: The mission is one of the factors. Depending on the mission and how it has been conceived, everything that is necessary for that mission to be carried out and depending on the availability of those factors, the mission will succeed or not. Another factor is personnel, which is a very important factor, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which has a direct effect on the mission, because it is very important to see what effectives the military commander has at his disposal, what the quality of the personnel is, is the personnel trained and educated and capacitated for the numerous duties he has in accordance with the rules within a military unit. Then comes the question of supply. This is another factor which, like the personnel factor, affects the success of the mission. Without logistics and without supplies for any military unit, a mission cannot be accomplished. By way of example, if there is no regular food supplies, clothing, footwear, weapons, ammunition, fuel, et cetera, then the mission will not be accomplished. And even if it is, it will be of lesser quality in proportion to the shortage of these supplies. Another factor is communications, which have a very important impact on the mission. It is common knowledge in all the armies in the world that communications in the most general sense among units is like the bloodstream in a human body. And if that is lacking, there can be no life. If a unit is -- has no communications or very poor communications, this will adversely effect the accomplishment of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like -- not that I want to interrupt you, but I would like to know how the factor that you've just mentioned, these factors, how do they impact on the commander's ability to exercise his command, or on his thinking. And let's, to begin, by -- you mentioned communication. How does that impact on a commander's ability to perform and to accomplish his mission?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: To make myself quite clear, I have to give you two examples: A normal situation, and a situation such as it was during the war in Bosnia. In a normal situation, every senior leader has regular, complete, and organised communications within the structure of his unit, starting from the plans to the technical means of communication that he has at his disposal in the unit. Under such conditions, every unit leader, having such means of communications at his disposal, has the necessary preconditions to fulfil his mission well. In another case, in conditions of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when virtually all the leaders of a military unit not only were lacking means but they did not even have plans, and having no means of communication or plans, that meant that at the beginning he didn't have the necessary formation, that is, the unit itself, because for plans and means of communications to be established, you need first to have a structure, because of the very large shortage of means of communications needed in large numbers, every military leader is forced to bridge this shortage diagonally with his superiors, as well as with his subordinates within the chain of command, and this forces every military leader in such a situation to resort to more primitive forms of communications. And this, again, requires far more manpower, et cetera, et cetera, and this directly impacts the quality of the accomplishment of the mission of each military leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if a commander -- you mentioned earlier that personnel was a factor which had an impact on his decision-making. How would personnel resources have a direct influence on the ability of the commander to make decisions?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I believe every aspect of society, and in the army as well, as an entity in society, everything starts with the human resources. Without good quality human resources, there can be no proper mission accomplishment. I can give you an example: All military formations in all the armies in the world today have highly sophisticated weaponry, equipment, and a wide variety of weapons, and to man them one needs trained personnel. If the military leader lacks such personnel for him to be able to accomplish the assigned mission, he must again resort to his own initiative and ingenuity as to various ways of bridging that gap in order to accomplish his mission, which has a direct bearing on the success of the mission, not to mention the quality of that success. If a military leader does not have professional and trained officers in the chain of command, many questions will arise, starting from the very ability of the chain of command to function, both upwards and downwards, et cetera; whereas, on the other hand, if there is trained and professional officers in the chain of command, then there is a probability that every military leader will, to the highest degree possible, achieve his functions as a military leader through the chain of command, both downwards and upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if a commanding officer of a corps has problems in his area of responsibility in the form of roads being blocked and his freedom of movement is limited, how would that affect, in your view, his ability to exercise his command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Such a situation would have a highly negative impact on any military leader for the simple reason that every military leader in his area of responsibility would have to grapple with a major problem, the problem of dealing -- how to deal with it. Without communications in satisfactory numbers in the area of responsibility of a military unit, without good quality roads, it is very difficult - one might even say impossible - to carry out combat activities and, in the final analysis, to fulfil one's mission. If those roads are scarce and if on top of it they're also blocked permanently or occasionally, this would put every military leader in a situation that has no solution, a situation when every military leader would start thinking whether he should resort to force to deblock the roads if that cannot be achieved without the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, if I look at another example, such as the feelings of the population in the area of responsibility of the commander. How would this have an impact on his ability to conduct or exercise his command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Every military leader would like to have a clear situation in his zone of responsibility in wartime. He would like all the population in his zone of responsibility - I'm referring to the civilian population - he would like the population to support him and to support the army or, rather, the unit under his command. That would be an ideal situation. However, if that is not the case or if the situation is such as it was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where in many parts of the territory and in many areas of responsibility of military units the population was mixed,-- there was the Croatian population that mostly supported the HVO, was more or less in its favour, and was mostly present throughout the AOR -- or the AORs of any of the corps of the ABiH. For example, the Serbian population, which was more or less in favour or supported the Republika Srpska army, much of that population was scattered throughout the AORs of the ABiH's corps, et cetera. All of these people could have presented a serious problem at any point in time for each and every military leader because it was possible to relay various information and they could be fifth columnists at any point in time within the AOR of a military commander. And as a result, when talking about the relation between the units in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation they were in was very different from the situations encountered elsewhere in the world in the course of a war, if we're talking about the relation between the army and the civilian population. However, I believe that in trying to find the best possible solution, the military leaders in fact managed to find the best solutions and to avoid situations that could have been much worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, one last area I'd like you to explain to what extent it may have an impact on the ability of the senior military commander to conduct his mission is the enemy. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber whether this has an impact on the thinking and the decision-making of the senior military commander; and if so, for what reason?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The enemy is the key factor on the other side and has direct influence on the mission or, rather, on the decisions taken by all senior officers. How does this factor influence the mission of all military leaders? It does so in that it's very important to be able to have control over the -- over the situation in relation to the enemy. You have to know how strong the enemy is. You have to know the nature of the enemy, the enemy's identity. You have to know what sort of weapons and equipment the enemy has. It's necessary to know how the enemy is trained, where the enemy is deployed, what his mission is, et cetera, et cetera. To be more clear, I will go back to the mission that the enemy has. It's well -- a well-known fact that, for example, the mission of the Republika Srpska army or, rather, of the Army of Yugoslavia, was to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina in the first few weeks and to annex it to a Greater Serbia after having established political and military authority.
