This wasn't done immediately, so the mission continued and its objective was to take and occupy as much territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as possible. When the Republika Srpska army -- or rather, Belgrade and Banja Luka, the political leadership from that -- from those centres failed to carry this out in such a brief period of time and they even failed to carry this out in the course of 1992, at that point they started cooperating with the HVO -- or rather, with Mostar and Zagreb, and their objective was to reach an agreement on carrying out that mission. They joined forces, and by joining their forces, the HVO and the Republika Srpska army became one enemy force, and in fact two enemy forces that the government had to face. And after 1993, a third enemy appeared as a product of those two enemies, and that was Fikret Abdic in Bosanska Krajina. This tells you what the enemy was and to what extent senior officers must take into consideration enemy forces. If all these enemies of the government and Bosnia and Herzegovina were numerous, if you take this into consideration and the fact that their equipment and weapons were far more sophisticated than the equipment and weapons of the government's forces, if you take into consideration the fact that the troops and officers were better trained, et cetera, et cetera, then this shows you to what extent this influences the decisions taken by a military leader who headed one of the units that were part of the government's forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 -- or rather, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm going to give you one last example with respect to the enemy, General, and that is if soldiers of the enemy forces commit crimes either against the civilian population or against your own army. Would that have an impact on the ability of the commander to conduct his mission? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. You have just covered the importance of knowing the enemy in order to allow the commander to exercise his command. If the enemy is committing criminal acts against your own forces or against the civilian population, would this have an impact on the ability of the commander to exercise his command? And if so, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: A minute ago I said that everything influences decisions taken -- or rather, the accomplishment of all commanders' missions. With regard to what you have mentioned, this does have a significant influence on how the mission is carried out. Why? Because any crime committed by the enemy, whether it's committed against members of its own units or against the civilian population, also influences the way in which decisions are taken because if a crime is committed against the soldiers of one's own unit or against the civilian population, in such a case the civilian population is -- has a direct link to the troops from one's own unit because they're part of that population, because their family members, close family members or more distant family members, et cetera, and this creates a particular psychological state among the people, and people in such situations either try to react or react in a way that is not quite normal, probably because it's impossible to control what we might call fear or perhaps something else. And through the soldiers and other officers within the chain of command, this -- or among the soldiers and the officers in the chain of command, this is something that can be felt, and it goes right up to the top. Depending on the extent, the nature of the crime, this can have a very significant effect on the decisions or on the -- how correct the decisions are of military commanders when accomplishing his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a little earlier, General, you mentioned that everything has an influence on the ability of the commander to exercise his command. And we have discussed a number of factors. What I would like to know is: Do these factors reduce the responsibility of a commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No. According to the rules, according to the law, a commander's responsibility cannot be diminished, cannot be reduced in that sense, in the way you have just mentioned. However, all those circumstances that we have discussed and that we are discussing in fact indicate how complex the situation was, how difficult it was to accomplish one's mission, how difficult it was for a military unit to accomplish its mission at a given point in time, if it had such numerous problems of this kind. And by way of an example, I have mentioned the problems that I as the corps commander had or the 3rd Corps commander had and various other commanders in other levels of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This, in fact, shows that the situation that prevailed was extremely complex and all these numerous factors that influenced the decisions taken are factors which are the result of something else or of one as well as -- or rather, of the state. Many of these factors are factors that each military leader has to be aware of if he is to take the appropriate action and to take the appropriate decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move to another aspect of your report, which is the duties and the responsibilities of the commander. And I refer you to part 3 of your report at paragraphs 488 to 491. If you can have a look at this part of your report. This is where you discuss the responsibilities and the duties of a commander. And my first question is: Do you see a difference between the responsibilities of the commander, on one hand, and the duties of a commander, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: There is a difference between these two concepts. The concept of responsibility means the responsibility of all military leaders in two senses: Firstly, he is responsible to the lower levels down the chain of command, and there is responsibility -- or the responsibility that he has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to his superiors up the chain of command. This is a very broad concept, in fact. But this is more or less the key to the concept of responsibility. Whereas, the concept of duty or duties relates to many of the duties that in paragraph 491 of my report I have referred to and I have enumerated; although, the duties that I enumerated in this paragraph do not provide an exhaustive list. It's difficult to enumerate all the duties that a senior military officer has.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Looking at the responsibility of the commander towards the chain of command, how would you describe this responsibility of a commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: All military commanders, and in particular senior ones, have an established chain of command. This chain of command is established on the basis of the structure and establishment that has to be previously established. The structure and establishment are manned and this is how the chain of command is formed. All military commanders have the duty to act as an example, to set an example to all his subordinates in the chain of command. Each and every military commander must provide satisfactory conditions for life and work. He must provide all the necessary logistics supplies to his men in the chain of command, to officers and unit members. Each and every military commander through his chain of command must ensure that combat morale is at the best possible level. And each and every military commander must do everything that is necessary in order to ensure that discipline is at a maximum level in his unit. He must supervise and control mobilisation plans. He must supervise and control decisions taken at lower levels. He must establish a network -- or rather, communications within his unit, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to -- I look at your report at paragraph 490 and 491, and you explain the difference between the responsibilities and those duties that are listed there. But what I don't see in these two paragraphs is the legal responsibilities. Is there such thing as a legal responsibility, or where does the law fit in this scheme that you have described in these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try to be more precise. I look at paragraph 490 of your report, and you describe that there are for the commander a responsibility towards the state and that there is a responsibility towards subordinates. And then in paragraph 491, you list all the duties that a commander must accomplish or perform. But what is not there is I do not see a legal obligation. So my question is: Where does the law fit into these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The legal obligations don't constitute a particular item, a particular duty. All these duties are legal obligations. It's the legal obligation of each and every military commander to perform all these duties in accordance with the law -- or rather, in accordance with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What I would like to do now is with respect to paragraph 491, if you could just go down the list that you have in your report and explain what the commander exactly has to do with all of these duties. Because the list is quite impressive here. You have about three pages. Can you quickly go through each of them and tell us what the commander has to do with all of these items.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I'll follow the order here. Firstly, overseeing mobilisation. The corps commander - we're referring to the corps commander - in normal conditions, under normal conditions each and every corps commander would receive all the men that would have to be mobilised from the Ministry of Defence and its bodies that have to implement the mobilisation. The corps commander has the duty to ensure that there's a mobilisation plan and to establish where the mobilised men are to be received. Upon receiving the mobilised men at a given location, from that point in time the corps commander is responsible for the men who arrive and report to the unit. As far as the role of the corps commander is concerned in relation to this issue, the corps commander has in his staff as part of the corps command a particular body that consists of a number of officers whose responsibility it is to draft plans and to implement these mobilisation plans. The corps commander only authorises these plans and naturally has an influence on the quality of the plans drafted. From time to time, he checks this in a certain manner. Secondly, selecting the best officers and sending recommendations to the Supreme Command Staff for their appointment to certain command positions. Under normal conditions when forming a corps, by virtue of the existence of mobilisation plans that someone else has the responsibility of drafting, all the men would have already been deployed within the corps' establishment, starting from the officers and right up to the -- or right down to the soldiers. At the same time, all of those men would have been trained and educated and would be assigned to certain establishment duties that require certain skills within the corps. As not a single unit in the ABiH fulfilled those conditions, it was developing from scratch, if I may use the word -- under such circumstances, many, almost all commanders of the ABiH had to find themselves the manpower from the level of soldiers to senior officers, and I would even go so far as to say that by finding people, soldiers and officers, on the ground, they would propose them for certain appointments to higher echelons. Some people were even captured to be appointed to a certain position, and then one might ask to what extent they were capable of fulfilling such duties, et cetera, et cetera. Not to mention the fact that first the formations and structures and entities had to be formed from the corps downwards and then they had to man -- be manned with soldiers who had to be found, recruited to the units, leading or commanding officers appointed, get hold of certain quantities of weapons and ammunition, and only then engage in certain combat activities and the accomplishment of the mission assigned to each commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, before you -- you proceed further, I mean, I understand that you could describe each of these duties for -- in very -- in a very detailed manner. What I would like you to do for the Trial Chamber is to say what is it that the commander does in practice in reality for each of those duties. What is the role of the commander, the direct implication of the commander in accomplishing these duties, and based maybe on your experience in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The third in order: Creating a communication network. The corps commander, together with his subordinate organs in the chain of command, had to prepare a plan for communications, and then he had to find solutions, that is, to get hold of means of communications and to a high degree he also had to find the specialised personnel for handling the means of communications to establish some sort of a communications system in his unit. Next, to ensure training. In the corps -- in the corps of the ABiH, the minimum required was to have specialised personnel to do the training, to have the necessary resources for that training, and to have a location where the training would take place, and all the corps commanders of the ABiH had only a minimum of all these requirements. In fact, some of these things were totally lacking. Next --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if I can interrupt you. With respect to training, there is one question in relation to training I would like to ask you: Would you expect, based on your experience, to see a corps commander organise or supervise training at the company or battalion level, for example?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No, that's out of the question. A corps commander is a senior military leader, the commander of an operative military formation. Training at company level and even battalion level and to a great extent at brigade level is not the duty of the corps commander; it is the duty of people in the chain of command who exist in commands at lower levels. The corps commander, with respect to training, is responsible for the training of the corps command and for certain types of training in order to ensure better quality functioning of the corps command, and to some extent he may be involved in some types of training at lower levels. For example, when exercising command posts of brigades or, rather, training and exercises of commands. Everything else at lower levels is not the responsibility of the corps commander. He neither has to participate nor control it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And moving down your list, with respect to morale, what does the commander have to do personally with respect to maintaining the highest combat morale, and how is this important to him?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Combat morale of a unit is a very important factor, and in developing combat morale every commander is expected to set an example to others by his behaviour, the execution of tasks and duties, and to expect his subordinates in the chain of command to act in the same way. For the development of good combat morale, it is essential to determine the political and military goals of the struggle from the outset, from the very top military and political leadership of the state, for all the personnel in a unit to be provided with the best possible conditions for life and work and their daily duties, right up to and including combat assignments. Every commander is duty-bound in order to develop good combat morale to constantly ensure supplies, logistics for all the personnel in his unit. Otherwise, this has a direct adverse effect on combat morale. The unit commander is also duty-bound to continuously demand a maximum degree of responsibility from all his subordinates in the chain of command in all his units, which again has a direct impact on combat morale and its maintenance, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I go down your list, General, and I see at the top -- well, you may not have the same page number as I do, but in the English version I see "Transforming operative missions or guidance received from the Supreme Command into tactical aims and tasks for his subordinate units to carry out." What does that mean and what does the commander of a corps do in this respect?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Every order, and especially if it's a combat order, once received by the corps commander from his superior command, be it in writing or orally, he has to gather his corps command together and to the extent necessary to require the presence of other personnel at the meeting to pass on the assignment. He gives a certain time limit for the preparation of a proposal. After that, they get together again and they submit their proposals, each one within his own duties and responsibilities. The commander listens to these proposals and makes a final decision. He issues an order to draft the written order for him to sign. When that has been done, he has actually transformed the order received from the superior command - for instance, the Supreme Command of the ABiH - to the corps command and through that order, which he then forwards to subordinate units, operative groups or brigades, he is actually issuing orders to all those units regarding combat assignments. Lower-level commands act in a similar manner: Operative groups towards brigades, and brigades to battalions. And that is how such an order received from the General Staff or Supreme Command is transformed by the corps command into lower-level orders or assignments of a tactical nature, going down the chain of command to the lowest-level military units within the corps structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have one last question for you today, and we do not have time to go through all your list, but I counted 34 different duties on this list, which appears to me to be a pretty impressive list. My question to you is: Is a corps commander expected to fulfil all of these duties and you in yourself, as commander of the 1st Corps, did you accomplish all of these duties?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The duties that I have listed in paragraph 491 are the duties of each senior military leader. I have to say straight away that I did not, that I as 1st Corps commander did not fulfil all these duties. Why not? Precisely because of all the things that we have been talking about so far, because of all those objective factors which prevented me from fully carrying out all these duties. And if we want to see whether a corps commander has executed all these duties or not, the answer will depend on the extent to which these other factors of an objective nature existed, not due to the corps commander's lack of knowledge or insufficient efforts, but rather, due to other circumstance. To what extent those circumstances prevented the corps commander to fulfil all his duties completely, to what extent they had an adverse effect meant that he was unable to fulfil his duties completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. As the Presiding Judge mentioned, tomorrow you will not be testifying, but we will see you again on Wednesday for the next -- continuation of the examination-in-chief. Thank you, General. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, as you have just heard, you will be coming back on Wednesday for the hearing at 2.15. In the meantime, you will not meet with anyone, as you are not allowed to meet with the Defence counsel or the Prosecution. Of course, you can leave, taking your briefcase and all your papers with you, and we will see you again on Wednesday at 2.15. It is three minutes past 7.00. Thank you all. And we will meet again tomorrow at 2.15 with another witness appearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of March, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
